title: Define the smallest valuable release
summary: Decide the smallest version that real users can use and get value from, so you start learning as early as possible. Small does not mean broken: it should solve a real part of the problem well.

beginner: Go back to the user need and the main success metric.
List everything in the full idea, then ask for each item: does a user need this to get value the first time?
Look for a thin slice through the whole journey rather than one finished piece of it.
Write down what is in the first release, what comes next, and what is out for now.
Check the first release is still usable, safe, accessible and legal.
Agree it with the team and stakeholders, and say clearly what you will learn from it.
intermediate: Map the full scope against the user journey and identify the thinnest valuable slice.
Agree in, next and out lists.
Confirm the release meets quality, safety and accessibility standards.
State what the release will teach you and how you will measure it.
experienced: Choose the slice that tests the riskiest remaining assumption with real users.
Separate the release you learn from and the release you market; they are often different.
Hold the line on scope under pressure by tying every addition to evidence.
Plan the next two increments so stakeholders see the path, not just the first step.

canDelegateTo.task: Draft the in, next and out lists from the backlog
Check the slice still makes a complete, usable journey
Confirm the slice can be built and released independently

toolExamples.miro: Build a story map with the journey across the top and draw a line for the first release.
toolExamples.jira: Create a release version and assign only the first-slice stories to it.
toolExamples.linear: Use a project with a clear first milestone and move everything else to later cycles.
toolExamples.claude: List your features and ask it to suggest the thinnest end-to-end slice, then check it with your team.

definitionOfDone: First release defined as a thin, usable slice of the journey
In, next and out lists agreed
What you will learn and how you will measure it written down
pitfalls: Shipping something so small it gives no value or no learning
Building one perfect component instead of a usable journey
Letting 'just one more feature' creep back in

leaderView.good: First releases are the smallest version that real users can get value from, so learning starts early.
ask: Who will use the first release, and what value will they get?
What did we leave out, and why?
signs: The 'MVP' takes most of the year.
The first release can't teach us anything about value.

sources.title: Making sense of MVP (Henrik Kniberg, Crisp)
